opus-5.5.text:
I think the shift is less about replacing one thing with another and more about where the bottleneck has moved.

When we were focused on RL for reasoning, the core question was: can the model learn to think longer and more carefully on a single problem? You give it a math question or a coding task, it produces a long chain of thought, and you reward the final answer. The inference system there is relatively simple: one prompt, one long generation, one verifiable outcome. The challenge was mostly about making that long generation efficient and making the reward signal reliable.

Agents change the shape of the problem. Now the model isn't just thinking in one continuous stream; it's acting in an environment. It calls tools, reads results, waits for a compiler or a browser or a search engine, then continues. So inference becomes multi-turn, interleaved with external latency, and the context keeps growing with observations the model didn't write itself. That puts very different pressure on the system: KV cache management across turns, handling long contexts efficiently, scheduling when part of your batch is stuck waiting on a tool call, and making rollouts for RL training work when each trajectory might take minutes and touch real environments.

And the training side changes too. With reasoning, the reward is often clean: right or wrong. With agents, the task is longer-horizon, success can be partial, and the environment itself becomes part of your infrastructure. Building good environments, sandboxes that are stable, reproducible, and diverse enough, starts to matter as much as the model architecture.

So I'd say reasoning gave us the capability for the model to think deeply. Agentic systems are about letting that thinking connect to the real world and take actions over time. The reasoning ability is still the foundation; without it, agents just flail. But the engineering and research center of gravity is moving toward the whole loop: model, environment, tools, and the inference system that ties them together. I think the teams that treat that loop as one integrated system, rather than just a model plus some scaffolding, are going to make the most progress.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly contrasts the earlier single-prompt, long-generation setup with agent inference that is multi-turn, tool-interleaved, and subject to external latency and growing context.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the RL reasoning engine was really about one thing: making a single forward pass of thinking better. You give the model a hard problem, you let it think for a long time, you reward it when it gets to the right answer, and the model learns to search in its own head. That was the whole paradigm for a while, and it worked remarkably well on math and code, where the problem is self-contained and verification is clean.

But once you take that model out of the exam room and put it into the world, you notice the bottleneck moves. It is no longer "can the model reason correctly given everything it needs." It becomes "can the model figure out what it needs, go get it, act, observe what happened, and then update." Reasoning becomes one component inside a loop rather than the loop itself. That is what I mean by an agent-centered inference system. The unit of inference is not a response anymore. It is a trajectory.

That shift changes almost everything underneath. On the training side, the reward is no longer a single number at the end of a chain of thought. It is attached to a long, branching interaction with tools, environments, and sometimes other agents, and credit assignment gets genuinely hard. You also have to care about things the pure reasoning era could ignore: when to stop thinking and act, when to verify versus trust a tool result, how to recover from a bad step rather than confidently compounding it. Those are behaviors, not just capabilities, and you have to deliberately shape them.

On the systems side, inference stops being a stateless request. You have long-lived context, you have memory that persists across turns and sessions, you have tool calls that may take seconds or minutes, and you have to decide how much compute to spend at each step dynamically. So the serving stack starts to look less like a text generation service and more like an operating system for a model, scheduling thinking, acting, and remembering.

What I find most interesting is that the two eras are not in tension. The reasoning engine is the kernel. The agent system is what makes it useful. A model that cannot think deeply will make bad decisions in a long trajectory, and a brilliant reasoner that cannot operate in a loop stays trapped in benchmarks. The real progress in the next couple of years comes from co-designing both, so that the model learns to reason about its own process of acting, not just about the problem in front of it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the earlier single-pass RL reasoning setup from agent-centered inference, where the model must gather information, act, observe outcomes, and update across a trajectory.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a shift in what we expect the system to accomplish. A reasoning engine is mainly concerned with producing a good answer to a given problem. An agent-centered system has to decide what to do next, act, observe what happened, and adjust its plan.

RL remains important, but the scope becomes broader. Reasoning is one part of a loop that also includes tool use, memory, and interaction with the environment. The system needs to recognize when it lacks information, when an action failed, and when it should ask a person for help.

That changes how we think about inference. It becomes a sequence of decisions about where to spend computation and what evidence to gather. Sometimes more thinking helps; sometimes the right next step is a simple check.

The key question, then, is whether the system can reliably complete a task across that whole loop. A strong reasoning model gives us a foundation, but turning that capability into dependable action is a broader systems problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts answer-focused reasoning engines with agent systems that act, observe, and adjust, and says inference becomes a sequence of decisions about actions, computation, and evidence. This communicates a substantially different inference problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a shift in the unit we optimize. With an RL reasoning engine, the focus is largely on the model: given a problem, can it reason its way to a better answer? With an agent-centered inference system, the focus becomes the whole process: what should the model do next, what information does it need, when should it use a tool, and how does it know whether it has succeeded?

Reasoning still matters, but it sits inside a loop of action and feedback. A model can produce a convincing plan and still fail when it interacts with an environment. The agent needs to observe that failure, update its understanding, and choose another action.

That also changes how we think about inference compute. More thinking before every action is not necessarily better. Sometimes a small experiment or a tool call resolves uncertainty much more efficiently. The system has to learn where to spend its effort.

So I would see RL as an important part of this transition, rather than something we leave behind. The challenge is to train and evaluate the entire trajectory—whether the system completes the task reliably—not just whether an individual response looks like good reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts model-focused RL reasoning with agent-centered inference over actions, information gathering, tool use, feedback, and task completion, clearly describing a different inference problem.
